question: Where must the training and inference code of a SageMaker job live?

options.text: In a Lambda layer attached to the training job
options.why: Not how SageMaker works. Lambda layers package code for Lambda functions; SageMaker jobs run in containers.

options.text: Inside container images registered in Amazon ECR
options.why: SageMaker runs training and inference code inside Docker images, and ECR is the registry where those images are registered. Input and output data usually sit in S3, but code goes in the image.

options.text: In an S3 bucket, loaded by the notebook at run time
options.why: S3 typically holds the data and model artifacts. The code still has to be packaged in a container image.

options.text: Directly on the EC2 instance's root volume
options.why: You don't manage the underlying instance by hand. SageMaker provisions it and runs your container.

takeaway: All SageMaker models are hosted in Docker containers registered in ECR. Because containers are isolated and hold all their dependencies, you can run any script or algorithm regardless of language or runtime.

question: Which statement about deploying models in SageMaker is TRUE?

options.text: Every trained model must be deployed to a real-time endpoint before it can be used
options.why: False. Your notes call this out: not all ML models are deployed to endpoints.

options.text: SageMaker Training, Processing and Hosting are three names for the same underlying job type
options.why: They are distinct. Processing is data work, Training builds the model, and Hosting serves inference. Telling them apart is essential for the exam.

options.text: Training, Processing and Hosting cover different stages; not every model goes to an endpoint
options.why: Correct. SageMaker covers the whole E2E process (data processing, training, deployment, hosting), but each stage is a different capability, and a model doesn't have to end up on an endpoint.

options.text: SageMaker can only train and host models built with its own built-in algorithms, not custom containers
options.why: False. You can bring your own code in a Docker image, or use pre-built DLCs for TensorFlow, PyTorch, etc.

takeaway: Know the difference between SageMaker Processing, Training and Hosting. Your notes say SageMaker is the 'heart' of MLA-C01, so most questions touch it.

question: You enable Early Stopping (Auto) on an AMT job. Which condition must hold for it to work?

options.text: The training data must be stored in Amazon FSx for Lustre
options.why: Storage choice has nothing to do with early stopping.

options.text: The tuning job must have been started with a Warm Start parent
options.why: Warm Start and Early Stopping are independent configurations.

options.text: The algorithm must be one of the built-in tree-based algorithms
options.why: Not a requirement. If anything, early stopping suits NNs, which emit metrics per epoch.

options.text: The algorithm must emit the objective metric after every epoch
options.why: Correct. Early stopping only works for algorithms that emit the objective metric after each epoch (most neural networks do). It stops training when the metric isn't improving significantly.

takeaway: Early Stopping = Auto stops a training job if the objective metric isn't improving significantly. Benefits: reduces compute time and helps avoid overfitting.

question: You want to continue a previous tuning job, but this time on a NEW dataset. Which Warm Start type do you choose?

options.text: TRANSFER_LEARNING
options.why: Correct. TRANSFER_LEARNING lets you use a new dataset while continuing where the earlier tuning job left off.

options.text: IDENTICAL_DATA_AND_ALGORITHM
options.why: This type requires the same dataset and the same algorithm, so it doesn't fit a new dataset.

options.text: EARLY_STOPPING_AUTO
options.why: Not a warm start type. Early stopping is a separate AMT setting.

options.text: RESOURCE_LIMIT_INHERIT
options.why: Doesn't exist. Resource limits are default quotas, not a warm start mode.

takeaway: Warm Start uses one or more previous tuning jobs as the starting point so AMT 'remembers' which hyperparameter combinations to try next. It also lets you stop and restart tuning jobs.

question: A hyperparameter's range is 0.0001 to 0.1. What does the AMT best-practice guidance recommend?

options.text: Use a linear scale so the values are evenly spaced
options.why: With a range spanning three orders of magnitude, a linear scale spends almost all samples near the top end.

options.text: Use a logarithmic scale across the range
options.why: Correct. Your notes recommend logarithmic scales when appropriate, for example when a range runs from 0.0001 to 0.1, so each order of magnitude gets explored.

options.text: Widen the range to 0–1000 so the optimum can't be missed
options.why: The advice is the opposite: keep ranges as small as possible and don't explore crazy values if you already have guidelines.

options.text: Fix this value and tune other hyperparameters instead
options.why: Not a best practice here. Tuning is fine, just choose a sensible scale.

takeaway: Other AMT best practices: don't optimize too many hyperparameters at once, focus on the important ones, narrow ranges, and don't run too many training jobs concurrently.

question: Why does the AMT guidance warn against running too many training jobs concurrently?

options.text: It violates the default AWS Region quota for S3
options.why: Concurrency isn't tied to S3 quotas. The concern is about tuning quality.

options.text: Concurrent jobs always produce different objective metrics
options.why: Not the reason. Metrics aren't affected by concurrency itself.

options.text: It limits how well the tuning process can learn as it goes
options.why: Correct. AMT learns from finished trials to choose the next combinations. Many parallel jobs mean less feedback is available when each new one is chosen.

options.text: Only one tuning job per account is allowed
options.why: False. There are default limits on parallel jobs, but they're quite high.

takeaway: AMT doesn't need to try every combination because it learns as it goes. For jobs on multiple instances, make sure the correct objective metric is reported at the end.

question: Your AMT job hits a default resource limit (parallel jobs, hyperparameters, etc.). How do you raise it?

options.text: Edit the limit in the SageMaker Studio settings
options.why: There's no self-service toggle for these quotas.

options.text: Switch the job to spot instances
options.why: Spot pricing reduces cost but doesn't change the limits.

options.text: Delete and recreate the tuning job
options.why: This doesn't change account quotas.

options.text: Submit a support request to increase the quota
options.why: Correct. Limits are fairly high by default, and raising them requires a support request. AWS sets them to prevent overspending by people who don't know what they're doing.

takeaway: Resource limits cover things like parallel tuning jobs, number of hyperparameters and training jobs per tuning job.

question: In a SageMaker TRAINING container, where do you find the hyperparameters file and the input data channels?

options.text: /opt/ml/input/config/hyperparameters.json and /opt/ml/input/data/<channel_name>/
options.why: Correct. Config (hyperparameters.json) lives under input/config, and data is split into channels such as train, validation and test under input/data.

options.text: /opt/ml/model/hyperparameters.json and /opt/ml/code/data/<channel_name>/
options.why: The model directory holds model artifacts, and code holds your scripts. Neither is where these inputs land.

options.text: /opt/ml/output/hyperparameters.json and /opt/ml/output/data/<channel_name>/
options.why: The output directory is for results, including output/failure for errors.

options.text: /var/sagemaker/config/hyperparameters.json and /var/sagemaker/data/<channel_name>/
options.why: Not the SageMaker convention. Everything is rooted at /opt/ml.

takeaway: Training structure: /opt/ml/input/config, /opt/ml/input/data/<channel>, /opt/ml/model, /opt/ml/code and /opt/ml/output (with failure under output).

question: Where does SageMaker look for the model files inside a deployment (inference) container, and are they updated during inference?

options.text: /opt/ml/input/data, and yes, they are refined with each request
options.why: Inference doesn't use input channels, and models aren't updated while serving.

options.text: /opt/ml/model, and no, they are not updated during inference
options.why: Correct. The files updated during training are included there, but inference only applies the learned model. It doesn't change parameters.

options.text: /opt/ml/output, and yes, they update nightly
options.why: Output is a training-side directory, and nothing updates automatically.

options.text: /opt/ml/code only, since code and model are the same
options.why: Code and model artifacts are separate things.

takeaway: This ties to a general rule from your notes: training updates a model's parameters, while inference does NOT.

question: Where do failure details from a failed training job go?

options.text: /opt/ml/failure at the top level
options.why: The note corrects a diagram on this point.

options.text: /opt/ml/model/failure
options.why: The model directory is for model artifacts.

options.text: /opt/ml/output/failure
options.why: Correct. Failures go under output, separate from the successful output but within the same directory. Your notes flag the diagram as inaccurate on this.

options.text: They are only written to CloudWatch and never to disk
options.why: Not how the container structure is defined.

takeaway: Small details like this show up in scenario questions. Remember: output/ holds results, and output/failure holds errors.

question: In a Dockerfile for SageMaker training, which instruction defines train.py as the script entrypoint?

options.text: COPY train.py /opt/ml/model/train.py
options.why: COPY puts the script in the image. Copying to /opt/ml/code is the right location, and it doesn't set an entrypoint by itself.

options.text: RUN pip3 install sagemaker-training
options.why: This installs the SageMaker training toolkit. It doesn't choose the script.

options.text: FROM tensorflow/tensorflow:2.0.0a0
options.why: FROM selects the base image.

options.text: ENV SAGEMAKER_PROGRAM train.py
options.why: Correct. The environment variable SAGEMAKER_PROGRAM tells SageMaker which script to run. The script itself is copied to /opt/ml/code.

takeaway: Dockerfile flow: FROM base image, install sagemaker-training, COPY your code to /opt/ml/code, then set ENV SAGEMAKER_PROGRAM.

question: At inference time, which component runs your Flask app that makes predictions, and what sits in front of it?

options.text: Gunicorn runs several Flask app workers (predictor.py), with nginx as the frontend
options.why: Correct. The serve program launches Gunicorn, which runs the Flask application defined in predictor.py. nginx.conf configures the nginx frontend, and wsgi.py is the small wrapper used to invoke the app.

options.text: Apache Tomcat runs the Java servlet that wraps the model, with HAProxy in front
options.why: Not part of the SageMaker container structure.

options.text: Spark executors load the model and serve predictions, with a Hadoop gateway in front
options.why: Spark and Hadoop appear in the notes as data-processing tools, not as inference servers.

options.text: The same train program doubles as the web server, with no frontend at all
options.why: train/ is invoked when the container runs for training, and serve/ starts hosting.

takeaway: Image layout: nginx.conf, predictor.py, serve/, train/ and wsgi.py. You can use separate images for training and deployment or combine both in one.

question: Which of these are the SageMaker Deep Learning Containers (DLCs) pre-built frameworks, and how is distributed training supported?

options.text: Only scikit-learn and Spark MLlib, with distributed training handled through Spark
options.why: scikit-learn and Spark ML have their own pre-built containers, but they're not the DLCs.

options.text: XGBoost and LightGBM, with distributed training supported through MPI only
options.why: These aren't listed as DLCs in your notes.

options.text: TensorFlow, PyTorch, MXNet and Chainer, distributed via Horovod or Parameter Servers
options.why: Correct. DLCs are pre-built deep learning containers for those four frameworks.

options.text: Only TensorFlow is prebuilt, and it has no support for distributed training across instances
options.why: DLCs cover several frameworks and support distributed training.

takeaway: Other options: pre-built scikit-learn/Spark ML containers, extending a pre-built image, or bringing your own training/inference code in a Docker image.

question: For the MLA-C01 exam, how deeply do you need to know SageMaker's built-in algorithms?

options.why: Your notes say that depth is expected for the Machine Learning Specialty (MLS-C01), not MLA-C01.

options.why: Correct. Know whether an algorithm is powered by NNs/DL (batch_size, learning_rate and num_epochs matter) or is a simpler, traditional ML algorithm.

options.text: Only the algorithm names, since questions never ask what they are used for
options.why: The exam expects you to know what each does and when to use it.

options.text: Not at all, because the exam is focused entirely on Bedrock and GenAI
options.why: SageMaker is the heart of the exam.

takeaway: Memorize the use case of each algorithm, and which ones are NN-based. NN-based ones make batch_size, learning_rate and num_epochs important hyperparameters.

question: Which statement about training and inference in supervised vs. unsupervised algorithms is correct?

options.text: Inference keeps updating the model parameters in both cases
options.why: The opposite. Inference never updates parameters.

options.text: Unsupervised algorithms are trained on labeled data, while supervised ones are trained on unlabeled data
options.why: Labeled data is what makes training supervised.

options.text: Supervised algorithms discover hidden patterns in data without any labels
options.why: That describes unsupervised learning.

options.text: Training updates parameters in both; inference applies what was learned without updating
options.why: Correct. Supervised training maps inputs to labels, and unsupervised training uncovers inherent patterns. Inference then applies the learned mapping or structure to new data.

takeaway: Supervised: train on labeled data, then predict labels for new data. Unsupervised: learn structure in the data, then apply it to new datapoints.

options.why: Correct. Unified Studio (the SageMaker Platform) is a wrapper around SageMaker and Amazon DataZone. Look for SageMaker AI in the console. The exam covers SageMaker AI.

options.text: They are the same product; the console just serves it from different URLs
options.why: They're distinct. The platform wraps SageMaker AI and DataZone.

takeaway: Your notes use 'SageMaker' as a synonym for SageMaker AI.

question: An email has a date and subject header plus a free-text body. How is this kind of data classified?

options.text: Structured
options.why: Structured data has a defined schema in rows and columns. A free-text body doesn't fit that.

options.text: Unstructured
options.why: Unstructured data has no schema at all. An email's header fields give it partial structure.

options.text: Semi-structured
options.why: Correct. Semi-structured data has some structure (tags, hierarchies). Email headers are structured (date, subject) while the body is unstructured. XML, JSON and varied-format log files are other examples.

options.text: Columnar
options.why: Columnar describes a storage layout (like Parquet), not a data-structure category.

takeaway: Structured = defined schema, easy to query. Unstructured = no schema, needs heavy preprocessing (raw text, video, audio, images). Semi-structured = in between, more flexible than structured but less chaotic than unstructured.

question: Which type of data requires the heaviest preprocessing before you can query it?

options.text: Rows in a relational database table with a fixed schema
options.why: These have a schema and are easily queryable.

options.text: Raw media and raw text (video, audio, images, emails)
options.why: Correct. Unstructured data has no schema or predefined structure and may come in various formats, so it needs heavy preprocessing.

options.text: A CSV file whose columns are consistent across all rows
options.why: Consistent columns make this structured.

options.text: JSON files with a consistent set of keys in every record
options.why: JSON is semi-structured. Its tags give it some structure.

takeaway: This is why services like Glue crawlers matter: once unstructured data is cataloged with a schema, tools like Athena can treat it like structured data.

question: You need a drive you can mount on an instance (like K:\ or /images). Why can't S3 do this, and what should you use?

options.text: S3 can be mounted directly as a drive from the console; no other service is needed
options.why: S3 can't be mounted as a drive.

options.text: S3 is object storage, not block storage; use Amazon EBS for mountable block storage
options.why: Correct. S3 is also not file storage (you can't browse it like a file system). EFS or FSx provide file storage.

options.text: S3 is file storage, so Glacier is the right service when you need mountable block storage on an instance
options.why: S3 is object storage, and Glacier is an archival tier, not block storage.

options.text: S3 is already block storage, so use EFS if you need object storage instead
options.why: This is backwards. EFS is file storage.

takeaway: Object storage (S3) vs file storage (EFS/FSx) vs block storage (EBS) is a classic distinction.

question: According to your S3 101 notes, what is the maximum size of a single S3 object?

options.text: 5 GB
options.why: 5 GB is the cap for a single-stream PutObject upload, not the object size limit.

options.text: 5 TB
options.why: This was the old limit. Note your S3 Performance page still mentions 5 TB, but the S3 101 page lists a larger one.

options.text: 50 TB
options.why: Correct per your S3 101 notes: 50 TB is a HARD limit (memorize), and objects can range from 0 B up to it.

options.text: Unlimited
options.why: False. There is a hard limit.

takeaway: Heads-up: your Performance Optimization page still says S3 stores objects up to 5 TB. The S3 101 page (updated) says 50 TB. Treat 50 TB as current.

question: In March 2026 AWS relaxed a long-standing S3 bucket requirement. Which one?

options.text: Buckets can now be created without being tied to any AWS Region
options.why: Buckets are still Region-based.

options.text: Objects no longer need a key, because they are now addressed by a content hash instead of a name
options.why: Keys still identify objects, like a filename.

options.text: Buckets are now public by default unless you turn on Block Public Access
options.why: S3 is private by default for security.

options.text: Bucket names no longer need to be globally unique; account regional namespaces allow it
options.why: Correct. When creating a bucket you can choose the global namespace or the newly recommended account regional namespace. Under the hood a suffix unique to your account and Region is appended.

takeaway: S3 is a global storage platform that is regionally based and resilient: data is stored in a Region and replicated across its AZs.

question: Why use a bucket policy instead of an IAM identity policy to give another AWS account access to a bucket?

options.text: Resource policies can name principals outside your account, including anonymous ones
options.why: Correct. Bucket policies are very flexible: allow or deny cross-account identities, anonymous principals (public access), block IP ranges, or deny users who haven't enabled MFA.

options.text: Identity policies can't be used with S3 at all, only bucket policies can
options.why: They can allow or deny access to S3. Final permissions are the overlap of all applicable policies.

options.text: Bucket policies are the legacy mechanism that AWS recommends moving away from
options.why: The legacy mechanism is ACLs.

options.text: Bucket policies don't need a Principal element, so cross-account access is implicit
options.why: They do. A Principal is required in resource policies, unlike identity policies.

takeaway: S3 is private by default. The Principal element appears in resource policies but not in identity policies, where the principal is the identity the policy is attached to.

question: In a bucket policy statement, what does "Principal": "*" mean?

options.text: All IAM users in your own AWS account
options.why: That would need specific identities, not a wildcard.

options.text: Only the bucket owner's root user
options.why: The owner doesn't need a policy statement to access its own bucket.

options.text: The anonymous principal, i.e. public access
options.why: Correct. This is how a bucket policy grants access to unauthenticated users.

options.text: All AWS services acting on your behalf
options.why: Services are referenced with service principals, not '*'.

takeaway: This is exactly why Block Public Access exists as a failsafe against accidentally public buckets.

question: Of the S3 security mechanisms, which is described as legacy and which as a failsafe?

options.text: Bucket policies are legacy; IAM policies are the failsafe
options.why: Bucket policies are current resource policies.

options.text: ACLs are legacy; Block Public Access settings are the failsafe
options.why: Correct. ACLs are legacy. Block Public Access is a failsafe layered on top of the other settings.

options.text: Block Public Access is legacy; ACLs are the failsafe
options.why: This is reversed.

options.text: IAM identity policies are legacy; bucket policies are the failsafe
options.why: Identity policies are not legacy.

takeaway: Three S3-specific settings: bucket policies (resource policies), ACLs (legacy) and Block Public Access (failsafe). IAM identity policies apply too.

question: You turn on S3 static website hosting. What must you do so people can browse it, and what do you need for HTTPS?

options.text: Enable versioning on the bucket; HTTPS then works natively on the website endpoint
options.why: Versioning is unrelated, and the website endpoint is HTTP only.

options.text: Enable MFA Delete on the bucket, and add Route 53 in front to provide HTTPS
options.why: MFA Delete is unrelated, and Route 53 is DNS, not TLS.

options.text: Nothing; the site becomes public automatically, and HTTPS is already built into S3 website hosting
options.why: Block Public Access must be disabled, and HTTPS isn't built in.

options.text: Turn off Block Public Access and make content public; put CloudFront in front for HTTPS
options.why: Correct. Without CloudFront you can only reach the website endpoint over HTTP.

takeaway: Static hosting needs an index document and an error document (e.g. for a 404). Use cases: offloading media from compute, out-of-band failover pages, and simple blogs/portfolios.

question: You want to serve a static site at example.org from S3 using Route 53. What matters about the bucket?

options.text: The bucket must be named example.org
options.why: Correct. Bucket name matters here. You also create a DNS record in Route 53 pointing to the bucket.

options.text: The bucket must be in us-east-1
options.why: No such requirement is described.

options.text: The bucket must have versioning enabled
options.why: Unrelated to custom domains.

options.text: The bucket must be named with a random suffix
options.why: The opposite of what's needed.

takeaway: Custom domains require you to pay for the DNS domain. The default AWS-provided endpoint works without one.

question: You suspend versioning on a bucket that has many old object versions. What happens to those old versions?

options.text: They are deleted automatically once versioning is suspended
options.why: Suspending does NOT remove old versions.

options.text: They are moved to Glacier for free after the suspension
options.why: Nothing like that happens.

options.text: They remain in the bucket and you are still billed for them
options.why: Correct. Once enabled, versioning can never be disabled, only suspended. All versions consume storage, so 5 versions of an object cost like 5 objects.

options.text: They become unreadable until you re-enable versioning
options.why: They remain accessible by version ID.

takeaway: To remove old versions you must delete each old version (version DELETE), or download current versions, delete the bucket and recreate it.

question: Versioning is enabled and you send a standard DELETE (no version ID). What happens, and how do you restore the object?

options.text: The object is permanently deleted from every version and can't be restored afterwards
options.why: That is how a DELETE behaves when versioning is disabled.

options.text: A delete marker is created and old versions remain; remove the marker to restore
options.why: Correct. The marker 'hides' the object, so a standard GET returns nothing. Deleting the marker makes the previous current version current again.

options.text: Only the oldest stored version is deleted and the newest remains
options.why: Not how it works.

options.text: The bucket automatically switches to the suspended versioning state
options.why: Delete operations don't change the versioning state.

takeaway: A version DELETE (with an ID) removes that specific version permanently. If it was the latest, the second newest becomes current.

question: A default s3:PutObject is a single stream (up to 5 GB). Which statement about Multipart Upload is correct?

options.text: Split into up to 10,000 parts of 5 MB–5 GB each, uploaded in parallel; failed parts retry alone
options.why: Correct. This improves speed and reliability, especially for large objects and global apps. Transfer Acceleration is the other option for global apps.

options.text: Split into at most 100 parts, each uploaded one after another in a single stream
options.why: The maximum is 10,000 parts.

options.text: Parts upload in parallel, but if any single part fails the whole upload must restart from the beginning
options.why: That's the single-stream problem. Parts fail and restart in isolation.

options.text: It only works for objects smaller than 100 MB, where one stream would be too slow
options.why: It's meant for large blobs (100 MB and up).

takeaway: Single-stream disadvantages: a failed stream means a full restart, and speed is limited by one stream. The farther users are from the bucket, the worse it gets.

question: What does the 'curse of dimensionality' tell you about features?

options.text: More features always improve the model, so you should keep adding them
options.why: The opposite: more features does not mean better.

options.text: Features should be duplicated across rows to reduce bias in the model
options.why: Not related.

options.text: Categorical features cause the problem; numeric features are unaffected by it
options.why: Dimensionality is about the number of features.

options.text: Every feature adds a dimension, so selecting the most relevant features matters
options.why: Correct. Much of feature engineering is selecting relevant features, where domain knowledge comes in. PCA and K-Means can help reduce dimensions.

takeaway: Feature engineering = using domain knowledge to create better features. Your notes call it the 'art of ML' and the most critical part of a good implementation.

question: Income data contains a few billionaires that distort the average. Which imputation is better for missing values?

options.text: Mean replacement
options.why: The mean is distorted by the outliers.

options.text: Median replacement
options.why: Correct. The median is more useful when outliers distort the mean.

options.text: Always drop the whole column
options.why: Imputation exists to avoid losing data.

options.text: Replace with zero
options.why: This introduces its own distortion.

takeaway: Mean imputation is fast and easy and doesn't change the dataset's mean or sample size, but it's not very accurate.

question: What is a major weakness of mean imputation?

options.text: It shrinks the sample size, because every row that has a missing value has to be dropped
options.why: It keeps the sample size.

options.text: It becomes very slow on large datasets because it needs several passes
options.why: It's fast and easy.

options.text: It works per column and ignores correlations between features, e.g. age and income
options.why: Correct. It also only works for numeric features.

options.text: It can't be applied to numeric columns, only to categorical ones
options.why: It handles numeric features only, so the issue is the opposite.

takeaway: If age and income are correlated, simply imputing means muddies that relationship.

question: A categorical feature has missing values. Which simple imputation could work?

options.text: Most frequent value
options.why: Correct. Mean and median can only be calculated on numeric features, but the most frequent value works for categories.

options.text: Mean of the column
options.why: Not defined for categories.

options.text: Median of the column
options.why: Not defined for categories.

options.text: Standard deviation
options.why: Not an imputation method.

takeaway: Common problems feature engineering addresses: missing data, unbalanced data, outliers and data transformation.

question: Match the Hadoop modules to their roles.

options.text: HDFS = resource negotiation; YARN = storage; MapReduce = scheduling of jobs
options.why: Mixed up.

options.text: HDFS = parallel processing; YARN = storage; MapReduce = scheduling of jobs
options.why: Mixed up.

options.text: HDFS = distributed storage; YARN = resource negotiator; MapReduce = parallel processing
options.why: Correct. Hadoop Common/Core provides the libraries the other modules run on. MapReduce uses mapper functions (data to key-value pairs) and reduce functions (aggregation).

options.text: HDFS = job scheduling; YARN = parallel processing; MapReduce = distributed storage of the data
options.why: Mixed up.

takeaway: HDFS is distributed, so it's scalable and resilient (data replicated across nodes).

question: How does Apache Spark relate to a Hadoop cluster?

options.text: It can run on top of HDFS via YARN, replacing MapReduce for processing
options.why: Correct. Spark is an open-source distributed processing system for big data workloads.

options.text: It replaces both HDFS and YARN, so a Hadoop cluster is no longer needed
options.why: It uses them.

options.text: It's a closed-source AWS-only service that can't run on a Hadoop cluster
options.why: It's open source.

options.text: It can only run on a single machine, never across a cluster of nodes
options.why: It's distributed.

takeaway: This is why EMR bundles Spark, plus HBase, Presto, Flink and Hive.

question: Which EMR node type is a good fit for spot instances, and why?

question: What does TF-IDF measure?

options.text: How quickly a document loads, weighed against its total file size

options.text: The overall sentiment of a document, ranging from strongly negative to strongly positive
options.why: Not what it measures.

options.text: The total number of documents that are stored in a corpus
options.why: Not what it measures.

takeaway: TF = term frequency in one document. DF = how common the term is across all documents. IDF is the inverse, and a log is used because frequencies are exponentially distributed.

options.text: It assumes a bag of words; building one is much of the work (case, synonyms, typos)
options.why: Correct. Words can also be represented as hashes for efficiency.

options.text: It requires labeled training data before term weights can be computed
options.why: It's a statistical technique, not supervised learning.

takeaway: TF-IDF is an old-school technique from search: it surfaces documents most relevant to search terms.
